newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Novartis sales, outlook on target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Novartis sales, outlook on target.

text.p: Novartis AG, the drugs and nutrition group formed through the merger last year of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz AG, on Tuesday reported 1996 sales in line with expectations but forecast flat profits.
The Swiss-based company, the world's second largest pharmaceuticals group, reported 1996 sales of 36.23 billion Swiss francs ($25.26 billion), compared with a pre-merger 35.94 billion in 1995.
Sales in the core life sciences business, which will comprise the group after the planned spin-off of specialty chemicals, rose eight percent to 27.60 billion francs from 25.50 billion in 1995.

Novartis said that, excluding one-off merger-related exceptional income and expenses, it expected net income for 1996 to be approximately the same as the year before. The combined 1995 net income of Ciba and Sandoz was 4.2 billion francs.
Despite flat earnings, analysts said the forecast was in line with expectations and they remained very positive about the company based on the growth potential of its main businesses.
"I intend to keep Novartis on my buy list. It's my number one pick in pharma worldwide," said Michael Sjoestroem, analyst at Pictet & Cie in Geneva.
Sales growth in Novartis' pharmaceutical products for 1996 were slightly above some analyst estimates.

Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) analyst Birgit Kulhoff, who stressed that she only researches the life sciences operations of Novartis, calculated that fourth quarter pharmaceutical sales rose 14 percent against a three percent third-quarter rise.
"These figures were above expectations mainly because the drop in sales of Voltaren is slowing and Lamisil and Miacalcic growth is accelerating," Kulhoff said.
Lamisil, used to treat fungal nail and skin infections, posted 1996 sales growth of 50 percent, thanks said Novartis to the successful U.S. launch of the drug in tablet form.
Miacalcic, an osteoporosis drug, experienced a 30 percent sales growth.

Kulhoff said the group's nutrition business growth was higher than expected in the fourth quarter, due in part to a recovery by baby food maker Gerber in the U.S. Sales in Poland were also strong, she added.

Bank Julius Baer analyst Beat Alpiger said the eight percent rise in life sciences sales was about one percent higher than expected, due mainly to the greater than expected positive effect of a weakening Swiss franc.
While pharmaceutical sales growth, at nine percent, was better than expected, it was still below the 13 percent sales gain reported by Swiss rival Roche Holding AG.
"It's still not as big as the increases that Roche showed...so we have to wait and see Ciba's new products becoming sold on a broader basis," Alpiger said.
Analysts all maintained buy recommendations on the stock, based on good growth potential for 1997 and 1998. Novartis shares were up 14 francs at 1,600 at midday.

Sjoestroem at Pictet forecast a year-end share price of about 1,900 francs. Alpiger targeted 1,800 francs within a 12 to 15 month timeframe, but cautioned he was not too aggressive because profit margins were not particularly high, especially when compared to Roche.
"The potential is definitely there for 1997 and 1998 as the synergies come through which are not yet discounted in the current valuation," he said.
Kulhoff was also cautious, saying: "The company is very clearly in a restructuring phase, but we expect it to be an outperformer."
($1=1.4344 Swiss Franc)
